Fake Ray-Ban Website Scam UK: Spot a Copycat Store

Scammers are cloning Ray-Ban's website to trap UK customers — but there are simple ways to tell the real site from the fake.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-20 · Updated 2026-07-30 · 9 min read

Quick answer: A very low Ray-Ban price is a warning, not proof: Ray-Ban itself currently advertises reductions on selected styles. Type ray-ban.com yourself, compare the exact model, check a claimed physical shop in Ray-Ban's locator, and use Ray-Ban's report-fakes form for a suspicious website or listing. Keep any received goods and packaging as evidence.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

A very low price is a warning sign, not a verdict

Counterfeiters copy branding, photography and increasingly the packaging, and the low number is the whole pitch. What that number cannot do is settle the question by itself, because Ray-Ban discounts too: its current UK terms of sale advertise reductions of up to 50% on selected styles. A figure well under the usual one is a reason to stop and check rather than a finding you can act on.

Treat the price as the trigger for the checks instead of the answer to them. Note the exact model on offer — the model number, the frame colour, the lens — then reach Ray-Ban's own site by typing ray-ban.com and find that model there. A gap far wider than anything Ray-Ban itself is advertising, on a seller you cannot otherwise verify, is the combination that should end the purchase. On its own, though, no price authenticates or condemns a particular pair of sunglasses.

What the UK store locator can and cannot confirm

Ray-Ban is an EssilorLuxottica brand and it publishes a UK store locator. That locator does one narrow job well: it confirms that a physical shop a seller names is actually a listed Ray-Ban location. It does not do the wider jobs a seller would like you to assume. It does not show that an unrelated web address belongs to a listed shop, and it is not a complete register of every authorised online seller.

So take a locator match as one piece of evidence, then finish the job separately:

  • Look the shop up independently and obtain its contact details for yourself, rather than using the ones printed on the site you are assessing.
  • Ring or email the shop on those independently obtained details and ask whether the website is theirs.
  • Where a site claims an online affiliation with the brand, ask Ray-Ban Customer Care to confirm it.

A partner badge, a certificate graphic or a registration number dropped into a footer is a claim a site has made about itself. None of it is verification, and none of it substitutes for a check you carried out from the brand's side.

A documented 2016 social-media campaign, and the current picture

Security researchers at ESET documented one version of this in detail in 2016. In the Facebook campaign they observed, posts spread through compromised accounts and tagged the account holder's friends so a link read as a personal recommendation; advertised discounts ran as high as 90%; and some of the checkout pages sent card details without encryption. That is a historical example of the mechanism, not a description of what any particular advert is doing today.

For the current picture Ray-Ban's own FAQ is the better source. It says counterfeiters operate through websites, marketplaces and social media, and it describes account compromise and misuse of personal data among the harms. Two habits follow from that. Ask a friend on a different channel whether they really posted a sale link before you trust it. And treat a warehouse sale, closing-down sale or clearance event that exists only inside a social feed, with nothing about it on Ray-Ban's own site, as unverified until you have checked it there.

Physical tells are supporting evidence, never a conclusive test

There is no visual inspection on this page that will authenticate a pair of sunglasses, and it is worth being sceptical of any page that offers one.

Ray-Ban does say that an SKU is usually printed inside the left temple, and it uses that code in its own support process. Checking the code against the same model on the official site is worth doing, and a mismatch is a genuine warning. A matching code is not proof of provenance — a code can be reproduced like anything else printed on a frame.

The same limit applies to etching, hinge feel, frame weight and what is in the box. An inconsistency there is supporting evidence worth taking seriously; a clean pass is not a certificate. If you are genuinely unsure what you are holding, ask the seller for evidence of where the pair came from, and ask Ray-Ban Customer Care what it can tell you about the model. Provenance is the more answerable question, and it is answered by checking the seller rather than by squinting at a lens.

Limit what a bad outcome costs you

NCSC guidance on shopping and paying safely online covers the part of an eyewear purchase you control most. Before a card number goes into a site you have not verified:

  • Reach the site by typing its address, not by following an advert, an email or a social post.
  • Use a payment route that leaves you somewhere to go. A shop insisting on bank transfer, cryptocurrency or gift-card codes has removed your recourse deliberately.
  • Set a password you use nowhere else if the site makes you create an account.
  • Look for named company details, a stated returns address and a complaints route. Be wary where a single web form is the only way to reach anybody.

None of that authenticates the sunglasses. It reduces what a wrong decision costs, which is a different objective and a far more achievable one.

If a pair has already arrived

Keep the frames, the case, the packaging and any printed insert, and photograph the listing and the advert before both disappear. With counterfeits the goods themselves are the evidence.

Citizens Advice says a buyer has a legal right to a full refund for counterfeit goods within 30 days of paying, with different remedies after that window closes. Its guidance page is written as advice for England and offers separate versions for Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, so read the one for your own region rather than treating a single page as a UK-wide route. Citizens Advice also points debit-card users towards chargeback and eligible credit-card users towards Section 75.

For consumer advice, contact the service GOV.UK lists for your nation: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262. GOV.UK’s consumer-rights guidance separately says the appropriate helpline can refer a complaint to local Trading Standards or share complaint information with another enforcement authority; whether anyone investigates or takes action depends on the case.

Eyewear prices sit right on the Section 75 boundary, so read that carefully. A Section 75 claim under the Consumer Credit Act 1974 may be available, not guaranteed. It turns on three things: credit funded the purchase, the required credit-to-supplier relationship exists, and the cash price — per item, or per qualifying set — came to more than £100 and no more than £30,000. So a £140 pair charged directly to a qualifying credit arrangement may be covered, while a £96 pair falls under the price floor.

A high enough figure plus a credit card is not a guarantee; MoneyHelper's guidance on card protection explains what the arrangement itself has to look like. Chargeback is worth raising either way, though card schemes rather than statute set its rules and deadlines.

Our scam recovery checklist covers the card, account and identity steps in sequence.

Reporting a fake Ray-Ban shop

Ray-Ban runs its own route for reporting a suspicious listing, website, social profile or post: a report-fakes form linked from its FAQ. Reach it by typing ray-ban.com and following the brand's own links, never by clicking anything inside the advert. Ray-Ban's FAQ says Luxottica has requested takedowns and works with customs and law enforcement, so a brand report is worth making — alongside the public routes rather than instead of them.

  • Submit the web address itself to the NCSC, using its scam-website reporting form.
  • Complain to the Advertising Standards Authority about a paid advert, and flag the post inside whichever platform served it.
  • Forward a phishing email to report@phishing.gov.uk.
  • Where money has gone: Report Fraud, at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040. Scottish readers report instead to Police Scotland, on 101.

Frequently asked questions

Could £29 Ray-Bans ever be a real clearance deal?

It is a strong warning sign rather than a verdict. Ray-Ban's UK terms of sale currently advertise reductions of up to 50% on selected styles, so genuine discounts do exist, but a figure far below anything Ray-Ban itself offers, from a seller you cannot verify, is a reason to stop rather than to buy. Compare the exact model on ray-ban.com and verify the seller before paying.

How much does the Ray-Ban store locator prove about a seller?

That a physical shop it lists exists, and little more. The locator does not show that a web address belongs to a listed shop, and it is not a full register of authorised online sellers. Look the shop up independently, ask it on contact details you obtained yourself whether the site is theirs, and ask Ray-Ban Customer Care to confirm any claimed online affiliation.

The sale link came from a friend's account, so is it safe?

Not necessarily. ESET documented a 2016 Facebook campaign that spread through compromised accounts and tagged the holder's friends so posts read as personal recommendations, and Ray-Ban's current FAQ says counterfeiters still work through social media. Message your friend on a different channel and ask whether they actually shared it.

Can I tell a fake from the etching, hinges and weight?

Not conclusively. Ray-Ban says an SKU is usually inside the left temple and uses it in its own support process, so checking that code against the official site is worthwhile and a mismatch is a real warning. A matching code is still not proof of provenance, and marking or packaging inconsistencies are supporting evidence rather than a verdict. If you are unsure, ask the seller for evidence of origin and ask Ray-Ban Customer Care.

The sunglasses are clearly counterfeit. What refund can I ask for?

Citizens Advice says you have a legal right to a full refund for counterfeit goods within 30 days of paying, with different remedies later. That page is written as advice for England, so read the Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland version if that is where you live. Keep the frames and packaging, and report it to your nation's consumer service, which may share suitable complaint information with Trading Standards.

How do I report a fake Ray-Ban site to the brand?

Ray-Ban publishes a report-fakes form for a suspicious listing, website, social profile or post, linked from its FAQ. Reach it by typing ray-ban.com yourself. Send the address to the NCSC as well, and take a paid advert both to the Advertising Standards Authority and to the platform that ran it.
